## 1. Identification Strategy
Primary strategy: Event-study difference-in-differences (DID) at the worker level, exploiting the quasi-exogenous timing of job loss induced by firm-level mass layoffs.

Rationale:
- Your panel links workers to firms and time, allowing worker fixed effects to purge time-invariant selection and calendar-time fixed effects to absorb aggregate shocks.
- Mass layoffs (large, sudden firm contractions) are plausibly exogenous to any one high-tenure worker’s idiosyncratic productivity or match quality, making them suitable to identify causal earnings losses from displacement.
- An event-study DID quantifies dynamics: pre-trends before separation, the immediate loss, and persistence.
- Heterogeneity by industry and local labor markets can be accommodated by interactions or by saturating with industry-by-time and county-by-time fixed effects.
- A complementary analysis on “non-mass-layoff” separations helps bound/selectivity-bias: we expect stronger pre-trends and more endogeneity in this group, so these estimates are interpreted with more caution.

Secondary, robustness strategy: Instrumental variables (IV) for separation using firm-level mass-layoff status (firm-year indicator that employment has fallen >30% below late-1970s peak). This isolates the component of separation driven by firm contraction, as an alternative to defining treatment on the displaced sample itself. We implement 2SLS at the worker-quarter level for levels of earnings, using worker FE and time FE.

## 2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable:
  - Main: An indicator that a worker experiences an involuntary separation (absorbing state) in quarter q0, where the separation occurs at a firm that has entered “mass-layoff” status (annual employment ≤ 70% of the firm’s 1977–1979 peak) by the separation year. Treated workers are the 6+ year-tenure separators from such firms, 1980–1986.
  - Secondary: Any separator (including non-mass-layoff) as a separate analysis.

- Control group (counterfactual earnings path):
  - Primary controls: High-tenure workers continuously employed at firms that never reach mass-layoff status during 1974–1986 and who are continuously employed through the relevant event windows. These controls share similar tenure structure, age range, and face the same aggregate shocks. In preferred specifications we further balance by:
    - industry (4-digit SIC) and county, and
    - matching or weighting on pre-event outcomes (earnings levels and trends) to ensure parallel trends.
  - Alternative controls: “Not-yet-treated” workers from pre-event windows in the event-study DID. We will also report estimates restricted to the mass-layoff subsample, where identification is tighter.

- Treatment timing / event date:
  - Event date is the worker’s separation quarter q0. Event time k = quarter − q0. We estimate dynamic effects for k ∈ {−12, …, +16} (adjustable based on support), omitting k = −1 as pre-period reference.

- IV (robustness):
  - First stage: Individual separation_it instrumented with firm mass-layoff status in year t interacted with high tenure, controlling for worker FE and time FE. LATE is the effect for separations driven by mass layoffs.

- No RDD is proposed.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends: Absent displacement, treated workers’ earnings would have evolved like the controls. Plausibility:
  - For mass-layoff separations, firm-wide shocks rather than individual performance drive timing, improving plausibility.
  - We will test this with pre-event leads and by balancing on pre-trends using matching/weights.
- Limited anticipation: Workers cannot perfectly time behavior in ways that contaminate pre-period earnings far in advance. Plausibility:
  - Mass layoffs sometimes follow announced downturns, so mild pre-trends (e.g., overtime cuts) are possible; the event study will reveal any anticipatory declines. We interpret k ≤ −3 cautiously.
- SUTVA/no interference: One worker’s displacement does not directly affect a control’s earnings path after conditioning on county-by-time and industry-by-time shocks. Plausibility:
  - Local spillovers from large plant closures exist; we mitigate by saturating with county×time (and industry×time) fixed effects, absorbing coincident local demand shocks.
- Stable composition/measurement: The outcome (quarterly earnings) includes zeros during nonemployment in the UI-covered sector, avoiding selection out of the outcome when displaced. Plausibility:
  - Some workers may leave the PA UI system (out-migration or self-employment). We address via bounds and robustness restricting to individuals with continued UI coverage spells and by IHS transform sensitivity.
- Exogeneity of instrument (for IV robustness): Conditional on FE and time-varying controls, firm mass-layoff status affects worker earnings only through separation. Plausibility:
  - Reasonable for the individual-level margin; any residual direct effects of firm distress on stayers’ wages are addressed by firm pre-trends controls/industry×time FE and by using worker FE.

## 4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
- Threat 1: Endogenous selection and pre-trends (especially for non-mass-layoff separations).
  - Remedy: Focus primary causal interpretation on mass-layoff separations; present full event-study leads; reweight or match on pre-1979 to pre-q0 earnings levels and trends; drop treated units with strong pre-trends in sensitivity; include UI-claim-based definition of involuntary separations as a stricter treated sample.
- Threat 2: Local labor market shocks contemporaneous with separations (differential trends).
  - Remedy: Include county×quarter (or county×year) fixed effects and 2-digit (or 4-digit if feasible) SIC×year FE; alternatively, control for county-quarter unemployment rates. The control group composition is restricted to similar industry–county cells to the extent possible.
- Threat 3: Attrition from PA UI records (out-of-state jobs, self-employment) leading to mechanically larger measured losses.
  - Remedy: Report bounds:
    - Lower bound: treat missing earnings as zero (main).
    - Upper bound: restrict to workers observed with any UI-covered job in PA 8+ quarters post event; compare magnitudes.
    - Sensitivity using IHS(y) outcome to downweight zeros; and using administrative UI claims to flag continued attachment.

## 5. R Code Outline
Note: This is an outline with executable code blocks; adjust file names/variable names to your actual schema.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # feols with sunab for event-study DID
library(ggplot2)
library(MatchIt)      # optional matching
library(sandwich)

# 1) Load data (assumes CSVs)
# workers_q: person_id, quarter (YYYYQ), firm_id, earnings (quarterly), yob, sex, hire_year_1974_dummy, tenure_yrs_1974based
# firms_y: firm_id, year, emp_annual, sic4, county
# ui_claims: person_id, claim_qtr (YYYYQ), sep_reason (if available)

workers_q <- fread("workers_quarterly.csv")      # quarterly UI earnings matched to firm
firms_y   <- fread("firms_annual.csv")           # annual firm employment + SIC + county
ui_claims <- fread("ui_claims.csv")              # optional for involuntary separations

# 2) Basic cleaning and time variables
# Create numeric time index for quarters (e.g., 1974Q1 = 1, ...)
parse_qtr <- function(q) {
  # expects format "YYYYQ#"
  yr <- as.integer(substr(q, 1, 4))
  qt <- as.integer(substr(q, 6, 6))
  (yr - 1974) * 4 + qt
}
workers_q[, t := parse_qtr(quarter)]
workers_q[, year := as.integer(substr(quarter, 1, 4))]

# Merge firm info to worker-quarters (use contemporaneous firm-year info)
firms_y[, peak_7779 := max(emp_annual[year %in% 1977:1979], na.rm = TRUE), by = firm_id]
firms_y[, ml_year := as.integer(emp_annual <= 0.7 * peak_7779)]  # mass-layoff status by year
setkey(firms_y, firm_id, year)
setkey(workers_q, firm_id, year)
workers_q <- firms_y[workers_q]

# 3) Sample restrictions
# Prime age by 1980–1986: born 1930–1959
workers_q <- workers_q[yob %in% 1930:1959]
# Employed at same firm since at least 1974
workers_q <- workers_q[tenure_yrs_1974based >= 6]  # adjust condition to reflect 6+ yrs by 1980 if needed
# Keep observation window 1974–1986
workers_q <- workers_q[year %in% 1974:1986]

# 4) Identify separations and event times
# Separation: last quarter with positive earnings at the baseline firm followed by 2+ consecutive zero-earnings quarters at that firm,
# OR a change in firm_id with no return to baseline firm (treat as separation from baseline).
# We'll focus on first separation from the 1974 firm occurring 1980–1986.

# Identify baseline firm as firm_id in 1979Q4 (or earliest observed if different rule is needed)
workers_q[, base_firm := firm_id[which.max(t[year==1979 & substr(quarter, 6, 6)=="4"])[1]], by = person_id]
workers_q[, is_base := as.integer(firm_id == base_firm)]

# Earnings at base firm
setorder(workers_q, person_id, t)
workers_q[, earn_base := ifelse(is_base==1, earnings, 0)]
# Identify separation quarter q0 from base firm: last positive earnings at base firm followed by no earnings at base firm
workers_q[, pos_base := as.integer(earn_base > 0)]
# Rolling next-period base earnings
workers_q[, lead_pos_base := shift(pos_base, type="lead"), by = person_id]
# Candidate separation when pos_base==1 and next period pos_base==0
workers_q[, sep_candidate := as.integer(pos_base==1 & lead_pos_base==0)]
# Define separation quarter as the last t with earn_base>0
sep_q <- workers_q[sep_candidate==1, .SD[.N], by = person_id][, .(person_id, sep_t = t, sep_qtr = quarter, sep_year = year)]
workers_q <- sep_q[workers_q, on = "person_id"]

# Restrict to first separation 1980–1986
workers_q <- workers_q[!is.na(sep_t) & sep_year %in% 1980:1986]

# Classify mass-layoff treatment: firm mass-layoff status in separation year for the base firm
# ml_year came from firm-year panel already merged
# Evaluate ml at base firm in sep_year
ml_by_person <- workers_q[year == sep_year & is_base==1,
                          .(person_id, ml_sep = max(ml_year, na.rm=TRUE),
                            sic4_base = sic4[1], county_base = county[1]),
                          by = person_id]
ml_by_person[is.infinite(ml_sep) | is.na(ml_sep), ml_sep := 0]
workers_q <- ml_by_person[workers_q, on = "person_id"]

# Keep treated (mass-layoff separators) and eligible controls (never-treated stayers at non-ML firms)
# Define adoption cohort g: sep_t for treated; g=0 for never-treated
workers_q[, treated_ml := as.integer(ml_sep==1)]
workers_q[, g := ifelse(treated_ml==1, sep_t, 0L)]

# Build a “never ML, never separated” control sample
# Flag never-treated stayers: no separation and base firm never reaches ML
# First compute firm ever-ML flag
firm_ml_ever <- firms_y[, .(ml_ever = as.integer(max(ml_year, na.rm=TRUE)>0)), by = firm_id]
workers_q <- firm_ml_ever[workers_q, on = "firm_id"]
# Identify stayers at non-ML firms
stayers <- workers_q[, .(ever_sep = as.integer(any(!is.na(sep_t)))), by = person_id]
workers_q <- stayers[workers_q, on = "person_id"]
# Eligible controls: ever_sep==0 and ml_ever==0 at base firm
workers_q[, control_eligible := as.integer(ever_sep==0 & ml_ever==0 & is_base==1)]
# Retain all treated_ml==1 units (across all quarters), plus control_eligible==1 units (across all quarters)
keep_ids <- unique(c(workers_q[treated_ml==1, person_id], workers_q[control_eligible==1, person_id]))
dt <- workers_q[person_id %in% keep_ids]

# 5) Construct outcomes and event time
# Outcome: quarterly earnings in levels; also alternative IHS(earnings)
dt[, y := earnings]  # includes zeros
dt[, y_ihs := asinh(earnings)]
# Time index is t; event-time for plotting
dt[, event_time := t - sep_t]

# Trim to an event-study window for treated and symmetric window for controls (Sun & Abraham stacks handle this)
win_lo <- -12L; win_hi <- 16L
# Keep all quarters for never-treated (g==0) and only quarters within window for treated
dt_trim <- dt[(g==0) | (event_time >= win_lo & event_time <= win_hi)]

# 6) Main event-study DID using fixest sunab (worker FE, quarter FE)
# Reference period k = -1
es_main <- feols(y ~ sunab(g, t, ref.p = -1) | person_id + t,
                 cluster = ~ person_id, data = dt_trim)
summary(es_main)

# Plot dynamic effects (omit k<=-2 overflow bins if any)
att <- etable(es_main, se = "cluster")
# Alternatively, use fixest::coefficients with sunab indexing for a more tailored plot
iplot(es_main, ref.line = 0)

# 7) Add covariates/heterogeneity
# Industry (2-digit) and county FE by time to soak up shocks
dt_trim[, sic2 := as.integer(floor(sic4_base/100))]
es_sat <- feols(y ~ sunab(g, t, ref.p = -1) | person_id + t + i(sic2, year) + i(county_base, year),
                cluster = ~ person_id, data = dt_trim)
summary(es_sat)

# Heterogeneity by region and industry: interact event-study with indicators
# Example: west vs east PA counties (assume a vector west_counties)
west_counties <- fread("west_pa_counties.csv")$county
dt_trim[, west := as.integer(county_base %in% west_counties)]
es_het <- feols(y ~ sunab(g, t, ref.p=-1):i(west, ref=0) | person_id + t,
                cluster=~person_id, data=dt_trim)
summary(es_het)

# 8) Robustness: (a) Alternative outcome transform; (b) Restrict to UI-claim involuntary separations
# (a) IHS outcome
es_ihs <- feols(y_ihs ~ sunab(g, t, ref.p=-1) | person_id + t,
                cluster=~person_id, data=dt_trim)
summary(es_ihs)

# (b) Restrict treated to those with a UI claim around sep_qtr (within +/- 1 quarter)
ui_claims[, claim_t := parse_qtr(claim_qtr)]
ui_flag <- ui_claims[, .(ui_sep=1), by=.(person_id, claim_t)]
dt_ui <- ui_flag[dt_trim, on=.(person_id, claim_t=sep_t)]
dt_ui[, treated_ui := as.integer(treated_ml==1 & !is.na(ui_sep))]
dt_ui[, g_ui := ifelse(treated_ui==1, sep_t, 0L)]
es_ui <- feols(y ~ sunab(g_ui, t, ref.p=-1) | person_id + t,
               cluster=~person_id, data=dt_ui[(g_ui==0) | (event_time>=win_lo & event_time<=win_hi)])
summary(es_ui)

# 9) IV robustness: instrument separation with firm mass-layoff status
# First-stage: sep_it ~ ml_year_it (at base firm and around sep_year), with FE
dt_iv <- dt  # ensure it contains base firm rows and ml_year
dt_iv[, sep := as.integer(t >= sep_t & !is.na(sep_t))]   # absorbing treatment indicator
iv_mod <- feols(y ~ 1 | person_id + t | sep ~ ml_year, cluster=~person_id, data=dt_iv[is_base==1])
summary(iv_mod)
```

Notes:
- The exact separation algorithm may need to reflect your administrative definitions; the above is a placeholder.
- If computationally heavy, replace county×year and SIC×year with county×quarter and SIC2×quarter only if feasible.
- For matching/weighting on pre-trends, compute mean earnings and slope over pre-event years (e.g., 1977–1979) and use MatchIt or entropy balancing to weight controls; then re-estimate es_main with weights.

## 6. Expected Results
- Direction: Negative and large. For high-tenure workers displaced in mass layoffs during 1980–1986:
  - Immediate annualized earnings loss on the order of 25–40% (roughly 6–10K 1980s dollars per year) in the first 1–2 years.
  - Persistent losses of 15–25% even 4–6 years post-separation, reflecting both lower reemployment rates and lower wages conditional on employment.
- Pre-trends: Small but nonzero declines in the 1–3 quarters before separation (reduced hours/overtime), substantially smaller than post-loss effects for mass layoffs; more pronounced pre-trends for non-mass-layoff separations.
- Heterogeneity:
  - Larger and more persistent losses in western PA and in heavy manufacturing (primary metals, machinery).
  - Smaller but still meaningful losses in expanding local markets.
- Conditional on re-employment in “similar” firms (same 4-digit SIC, same county, similar size): losses likely remain 10–20%, consistent with loss of firm-specific wage premia and tenure resets.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-study DID)
- C1: Parallel trends supported by pre-event leads (especially in mass-layoff subsample) = 1
- C2: Limited anticipation (no large pre-trends beyond immediate pre-separation dip) = 1
- C3: No interference/GE confounding after including county×time and industry×time FE = 1
- C4: Stable outcome definition with zeros for nonemployment; attrition addressed via bounds/sensitivity = 1
- C5: Correct specification and inference (worker FE, time FE, clustered SE at worker; balanced event window) = 1

Interpretation guide:
- Treat the mass-layoff event-study as the main causal result.
- Use non-mass-layoff separations to illustrate selection and upper/lower bounds.
- Report dynamics with transparent pre-trend diagnostics and heterogeneity by industry/region.
